noi_dung:
Investigating Chan Is the Means to Enlightenment

After Buddhism spread to China, it divided into five schools: Chan, Teachings, Vinaya, Pure Land, and Esoteric. Chan is meditative concentration; Teachings is doctrine; Vinaya is moral discipline; Pure Land is the Pure Land; Esoteric is mantra holding. This is the time of a Chan Session, so I shall speak only of Chan principle, leaving the other four schools aside for now.

Dhyana, translated as "cultivation through reflection," means constantly reflecting upon a single matter. What matter? The hua-tou. Examining "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" is called investigating Chan. In fact, investigating the hua-tou is itself just a discursive thought; only, we use one discursive thought to subdue discursive thoughts—"countering poison with poison"—taking one discursive thought to destroy many other discursive thoughts. Skill in investigating the hua-tou takes a long time to mature; hence the saying: "Only long investigation brings Chan."

"Investigate" is like boring into wood with an auger. Until you have bored clean through, you do not stop—you cannot quit halfway, for then all former effort is thrown away. In investigating Chan, the most important thing is the ability to endure. When patience reaches its peak, not a single idle thought may arise. When "not a thought arises," you can become enlightened. There is a saying:

"Atop a hundred-foot pole, step one step further."

That is, standing atop a hundred-foot pole, you still step one step further. Then "the worlds of the ten directions wholly appear." But this Dharma-door works only if cultivated in every thought at all times—no laziness, no laxity. In the Song of Enlightenment it is said:

Suddenly awakened to the Tathagata Chan,

The Six Perfections and myriad practices complete within;

In dreams, clearly there are the six destinies,

Awake, utterly empty, not even the great chiliocosm.

Meaning:

Suddenly awakened to the Tathagata Chan.

The Six Perfections and myriad practices, whole and complete.

Dreaming, clearly there are six paths;

Awake, all empty—no great chiliocosm.

"Sudden" means instantly awakening to a principle. As it is said:

Principle can be suddenly awakened to; practice is cultivated gradually.

(Principle may be understood in an instant, but practice must proceed step by step.)

As to "practice," we must cultivate step by step; as to "principle," we must understand it at once. When suddenly enlightened, we know where the well is and go draw water; before sudden enlightenment, we hear only the pulley's rope drawing water, never knowing where the well is. This analogy explains where the Buddha-nature comes from. How is the Buddha-nature realized? Realizing the Buddha-nature has no other method—only investigating Chan and sitting in Chan.

The Six Perfections are the Dharma-doors Bodhisattvas cultivate. Giving "carries across" stinginess and greed. Moral discipline "carries across" violation. Patience "carries across" anger. Vigor "carries across" laxity and laziness. Samadhi "carries across" scattering. Wisdom "carries across" delusion. Only when the Six Perfections are perfected can enlightenment come.

We are always dreaming. As it is said:

Human life, a single dream;

Human death, a dream's span.

In dreams, glory and honor;

Awake, a poor village still.

Day after day, ever dreaming,

Unaware of the yellow-millet dream;

Dreaming on, yet never knowing—

A wasted dream indeed.

Meaning:

The living: one long dream,

The dead: a dream one long.

Within the dream, rank and riches;

Dream over, poor and bare.

Day after day, always dreaming,

Never knowing the "yellow millet" dream;

Dreaming, yet never knowing—

A wasted dream indeed.

Dreaming, we clearly see the six destinies (heavens, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells); only upon awakening do we see that the great trichiliocosm does not even exist. Why? Because attachment is gone. With attachment gone, the myriad things "return to the origin"; how then could there be marks of self, others, living beings, or a life? All are gone! Hearing that the four marks are all gone, some dare not cultivate, mistakenly thinking: "Cultivate to the peak and people no longer exist, beings all vanish, no liver of life remains—then what? All work ends too, and I shall be out of a job!"

Must you have work to do? Then keep right on being upside down! When cultivation reaches the end of the four marks, you will "sweep away all dharmas, leave behind all marks," realizing the True Suchness of all things. As it is said:

Not a single dharma is set up; the myriad dharmas are all empty.

(Not one dharma is established; all things are empty.)

It will not do to merely say you understand this principle—we must truly realize the state where "not a single dharma is set up, all things are empty." Then there is no more suffering, only the enjoyment of peace.

People in the world, if not clinging to fame, clutch tightly at gain; if not attached to money, then entranced by beauty—and so cannot see through (appearances), cannot let go (of attachments). They wish to see through, wish to let go, yet cannot. Why not? Because in the mind a subtle ghost and a clever worm play tricks, and so in many matters we miss our chances—facing Avalokiteshvara, yet failing to recognize him. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva stands right before us, yet we go searching everywhere. That is precisely being ruled by upside-down discursive thoughts.

The word "investigate" in investigating Chan means to contemplate and observe. Contemplate what? Contemplate prajna. That is, in every thought, at every moment, observe yourselves right here (abiding at ease in yourselves), not others (abiding in others). Observe whether you are present here—if you are here, you can investigate Chan and apply effort; if you are not here, you are giving rise to scattered discursive thoughts and idle fancies. The body sits in the Chan Hall, but the mind races off to New York or Italy. Reaching everywhere, climbing on conditions—no longer at ease.

Contemplating at ease is being a Bodhisattva. Contemplating uneasily is being a common being. Contemplating at ease is heaven. Contemplating uneasily is hell. If we contemplate at ease, the mind not running outward, then we can "practice the profound prajna paramita." In investigating Chan, the body sits in the Chan Hall while the mind continuously, unbrokenly investigates—only that is truly practicing profound prajna, finding wisdom. Attaining great wisdom, we reach the other shore, the shore of liberation.

The secret of investigating Chan is "by day reflect, by night reflect" (investigating by day, investigating by night). Investigate what? Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigate today, investigate tomorrow. Day after day in the Chan Hall, "practice the profound prajna paramita"—but do not expect to taste the savor of Chan after only a short time. You must pass through a long, long time. Only with skill in "practicing the profound prajna paramita" can you "see that the five skandhas are all empty."

The five skandhas are also called the five coverings. "Skandha" means accumulation; "covering" means veiling and shrouding. Why are we not at ease, not liberated? Because we are shrouded by the five coverings! The five skandhas are form, feeling, cognition, formation, and consciousness.

The form skandha: what has obstruction is called form; what has shape is also form. If the form skandha is not empty, then seeing forms you are deluded by the dust of forms, hearing sounds you are deluded by the dust of sounds, smelling scents you are deluded by the dust of scents, tasting flavors you are deluded by the dust of flavors, touching things you are deluded by the dust of touch. If the form skandha were empty, then within there would be no mind, without no shapes, near and far no things. "Form" also means all kinds of beauty, looks that confuse the eyes so you cannot see clearly—hazy, like the blind. In the Daodejing it is said:

The five colors blind the eye;

The five sounds deafen the ear;

The five flavors numb the palate.

Meaning:

Five colors blind people's eyes,

Five sounds deafen people's ears,

Five flavors dull people's mouths.

All these come from delusion by the form skandha. Once the form skandha is smashed, mountains and rivers, lands, cities, houses are all empty—no more trouble. So while the form skandha is not empty, we remain attached to form. Attached to form, the delusions of views (the delusion of seeing) cannot be removed.

Delusions of views arise when, meeting states, craving and fondness start. States are form. Facing whatever state, giving rise to greed or fondness—that is attachment. Delusions of views have eighty-eight grades; sever them all and you realize the First Fruit of Arhatship. We who cultivate the Way must first sever the eighty-eight grades of view-delusions existing in the Three Realms, then sever the eighty-one grades of thought-delusions in the Three Realms.

Thought-delusions come from delusion about truth, giving rise to discrimination—failing to see all principles clearly. Severing all eighty-one grades of thought-delusions, you realize the Fourth Fruit of Arhatship.

The feeling skandha. "Feeling" is receiving and accepting, giving rise to sensation. When states come, with no thinking at all, you at once take them in and produce a sensation. Eating something, sensing it delicious—that is "feeling." Wearing fine clothes, feeling pleased—also "feeling." Living in a fine house, feeling delight—that is "feeling." Riding in a fine car, feeling comfortable—also "feeling." Whatever the body receives, however it senses it—all is called "feeling."

The cognition skandha: that is thought, ideas. Because the five senses contact and receive the states of the five dusts, all kinds of discursive thoughts and ideas arise. They flash into being and vanish, producing reflection upon form and feeling.

The formation skandha. Formation means shifting flow—moving and changing, now coming now going, now going now coming, never pausing, drifting on without stop. The impulse to do evil or good lies in the mind, yet ruled by discursive thought and reflection, it shows through the acts and gestures of body, mouth, and mind (all such acts belong to the formation skandha).

The consciousness skandha. Consciousness means discrimination; when states come, a discriminating mind arises. For example: seeing beauty, delight arises; hearing harsh words, dislike arises, and so on.

Smashing through the five skandhas, you cross beyond all suffering and hardship—no more calamity at all. Why do we suffer calamity? Because we have not yet cast off the two attachments: attachment to self and attachment to dharmas (all things and matters).

In Great Master Xuanjue's Song of Enlightenment it is said:

The five skandhas, floating clouds, empty in coming and going;

The three poisons, water bubbles, hollow in appearing and vanishing.

Meaning:

The five skandhas like drifting clouds, neither coming nor going; The three poisons like water bubbles, falsely appearing and vanishing.

The five skandhas never had any own-nature—like drifting clouds, suddenly there, suddenly gone. Not penetrating this principle, we remain forever shrouded by the five skandhas, unable to be at ease, unable to be liberated. The cultivator must smash the five skandhas. As clouds drift by, let them drift by; as they drift away, let them drift away. Pay them no heed, cling to them not. The three poisons—greed, anger, delusion—are like water bubbles, with no real substance. They arise of themselves and vanish of themselves, so do not cling to them. The "Song of Enlightenment" also says:

Realize True Suchness—no person, no dharmas;

In an instant, wipe out Avici karma.

If I used false words to deceive beings,

May I have my tongue pulled out for dust-mote kalpas.

Meaning:

Realize True Suchness—no person, no dharmas;

In an instant, shake off Avici karma.

If with lying words I deceived beings,

May I suffer tongue-cutting for Ganges-sand kalpas.

"True Suchness" is "no marks, yet nothing that is not marked" (no shape at all, yet nothing that is not it). It also means "sweep away all dharmas and matters; leave behind all marks and notions." It may be called "returning to the origin, realizing the pure own-nature." Reaching this state, there is neither person nor dharmas. Person and dharmas both forgotten. No more clinging to people, no more clinging to dharmas (things and matters) either. That is realizing the principle and substance of True Suchness. Then, in a single instant, all the karma leading to the Uninterrupted Hells, created through limitless kalpas past, at once wholly dissolves. Great Master Yongjia said: "If I used false words to deceive beings, I willingly go down to the tongue-pulling hells, suffering through kalpas as countless as dust motes."

In the Chan Hall, cultivate genuinely. Like reeling silk from cocoons, you must be patient, drawing each thread slowly, or it tangles. Do not fancy yourselves clever, seeking shortcuts, wanting to use science to become enlightened—that is idle fancy. If science could bring enlightenment, scientists would long ago have cornered it for themselves, enlightened long since, leaving no share for anyone else! Put away hazy notions; sincerely and properly investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Though your back aches, bear it; though your legs hurt, endure; enduring on and on, the moment will come when you become enlightened. As it is said:

Without one bout of bone-piercing cold,

How could plum blossoms fill the nose with fragrance?

Meaning:

Never passing through bone-chilling cold,

How could plum blossoms release their scent?

Take heed! Do not be too clever, only to be fooled by your own cleverness. Remember: a share of effort in cultivation is a share of skill. Cultivation is true skill, not "mouth Chan" (Chan in words only). Mere talk without practice does no good. "Mouth Chan" not only fails to help enlightenment—on the contrary, it obstructs. Hence:

"Not speaking—that is Chan."

A single thought of spiritual light can shine through heaven and earth—you are in no way different from the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods. Why can we not realize the Three Bodies, Four Wisdoms, Five Eyes, and Six Spiritual Powers? Because we common beings have too many discursive thoughts, and so wisdom is veiled, lightless—becoming ignorance. All day raising delusion, creating karma, and so undergoing bitter retribution in the round of birth and death.

The Three Bodies are the Dharma body, the reward body, and the response body (or transformation body).

The Four Wisdoms are the All-Accomplishing Wisdom, the Wonderful Contemplating Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality-Nature, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The Five Eyes are the flesh eye, the heavenly eye, the Dharma eye, the wisdom eye, and the Buddha eye.

The Six Spiritual Powers are the heavenly-eye penetration, the heavenly-ear penetration, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, spiritual travel, and the ending of outflows.

Only with no discursive thoughts at all can you realize these states. This is no abstruse philosophy or theory—just a natural phenomenon, realized through true skill. Nothing strange about it; most ordinary.

From beginningless kalpas past we have been veiled by ignorance, never meeting a Good Knowing Advisor to guide us, never knowing what understanding the mind and seeing the nature (awakening to one's own mind, thoroughly seeing the fundamental nature) is, never knowing what returning to the origin (going back to the source) is. We practice Chan precisely to understand the mind and see the nature, to return to the origin. Once liberated, there are no more obstacles or hindrances—far apart from all upside-down dream-like thinking—at last reaching Nirvana.

Chan Session, 12/1980
